jsnvu6-e182018-d1e106.summary: Rubric for Question 1 of d.24: whether God is the object of faith, referring to Aquinas.

jsnvu6-e182018-d1e119.summary: Argument that God is not the object of faith: faith and unbelief concern the same thing, but unbelief concerns other things than God, such as the resurrection of the dead.
claims: Unbelief concerns creaturely matters, so faith does too (objection)

jsnvu6-e182018-d1e135.summary: Second argument: faith corresponds to charity, by which not only God but also neighbor is loved; so faith concerns created as well as uncreated objects.
claims: Like charity, faith extends to created objects (objection)

jsnvu6-e182018-d1e147.summary: Argument for the opposite: every theological virtue has God for object, and faith is one (as shown earlier); and Dionysius (Divine Names 7) says faith concerns the simple, superexistent truth, which is divine truth alone.
claims: Faith, as a theological virtue, has God for its object

jsnvu6-e182018-d1e163.summary: Outline of the response: whether God is the object of faith, and under what formal aspect.

jsnvu6-e182018-d1e174.summary: First distinction: 'faith' is taken either according to its common formal notion—a habit of assenting to something on the authority of the speaker—or as the habit by which we assent to Scripture on the authority of God revealing it, the theologians' faith, related to the first as species to genus, not as opposed coordinate (as stated at the beginning of Book 1).
claims: Faith in general is assent on a speaker's authority
Theological faith is assent to Scripture on God's authority, a species of faith in general
concepts: faith in general vs. theological faith

jsnvu6-e182018-d1e200.summary: Second distinction: the object of faith may be what is believed or that about which something is believed, just as the object of science is either the demonstrated conclusion (complex) or the subject of the conclusion of which properties are known (incomplex).
claims: The object of a cognitive habit may be the complex proposition believed or the incomplex subject of which it is believed

jsnvu6-e182018-d1e226.summary: If the object is that about which something is believed, God is the per se and principal object of theological faith, since the principal object is that to which all believed things are attributed, and all held by faith are attributed to God. Taken thus, it is incomplex.
claims: God is the principal object of faith as that to which all credibles are attributed

jsnvu6-e182018-d1e252.summary: If the object is what is believed, it is complex: faith is intermediate between science and opinion, whose objects are conclusions; assent bears only on propositions; and believer and unbeliever differ not in grasping terms (God, one, three) but in assenting to complexes such as God being one in essence and three in persons. Among these, one is first believed, the reason for believing the others and the term of their resolution: that the Church is ruled by the Holy Spirit. We believe the articles because Scripture says them, and we believe Scripture inspired because the Church approves it, as Augustine says (Contra epistolam fundamenti: I would not believe the Gospel unless I believed the Church), excluding e.g. the Gospel of the Nazarenes.
claims: What is believed is a complex proposition
Believers and unbelievers differ only in assent to complexes, not in grasping terms
The first credible, to which all others resolve, is that the Church is ruled by the Holy Spirit
We believe Scripture inspired because the Church approves it

jsnvu6-e182018-d1e364.summary: Clarifies that the Church's approval of Scripture refers to the Church of the Apostles, filled with the Spirit and eyewitnesses of Christ's deeds and teaching (1 John 1; Acts 1 on the choice of Matthias), whose testimony approved the Scriptures. Gospels approved by that Church cannot now be rejected, as no similar cause exists, and whoever holds otherwise, of whatever status, is a heretic.
claims: The approving Church is the apostolic Church of eyewitnesses
Gospels approved by the apostolic Church cannot now be rejected
Contradicting the apostolic approval of Scripture is heresy

jsnvu6-e182018-d1e403.summary: Second article: some hold that the formal aspect of faith's object is being unseen, citing Heb. 11 ('argument of things not apparent'), Rom. 8 on hope, Augustine ('believe what you do not see'), and Gregory (faith has no merit where reason gives proof; things apparent produce recognition, not faith).
claims: Some hold that non-visibility is the formal ratio of faith's object

jsnvu6-e182018-d1e436.summary: Refutation, first two reasons: the formal aspect of a cognitive habit's object cannot be negative or privative, since privations and negations are known only through habits and affirmations, whereas the formal aspect is what the habit first attains. And the formal aspect lies on the side of the object, not the knower, whereas being unseen depends on whether the knower's act falls on it.
claims: The formal object of a cognitive habit cannot be negative or privative
The formal object belongs to the object, not to the condition of the knower
Being unseen depends on the knower and so is not a formal ratio

jsnvu6-e182018-d1e478.summary: Third reason: if being unseen were faith's formal aspect, being seen would be vision's, since opposed habits have opposed formal objects; but being seen is not prior to the act of seeing, being rather its result, so it cannot be vision's formal object.
claims: Being seen follows the act of vision and so is not its formal object
Hence being unseen is not the formal object of faith

jsnvu6-e182018-d1e507.summary: A possible fourth reason: everything considered by a habit is attributed to its formal aspect, and the habit's end is perfect cognition of its subject under that aspect; if being unseen were the formal aspect, faith's end would be to know God insofar as unseen and what pertains to him as unseen, which is absurd.
claims: Not all that faith considers is attributed to non-visibility
Faith's end is not knowing God insofar as he is unseen

jsnvu6-e182018-d1e540.summary: Non-visibility is a concomitant condition of faith's object in this life: its objects are not present to our intellect to be seen nor in their causes to be known scientifically, but presented only by Scripture's authority, which gives neither vision nor science. The cited authorities speak of faith in via in this sense. Whether this condition can be separated from faith's object is left to d.31.
claims: Being unseen is a concomitant condition, not the formal ratio, of faith's object in via
Faith's objects are presented by scriptural authority, which yields neither vision nor science

jsnvu6-e182018-d1e570.summary: Formal aspect of faith's object: taken as that about which things are believed, it is the aspect under which everything believed is attributed to God, as determined at the start of Book 1 regarding the subject of theology. Taken as the complexes believed, no further formal aspect need be sought, just as in science one seeks the formal aspect of the subject, not of the conclusions; but if their formal aspect means the middle of assent, it is the divine authority governing the Church and revealing Scripture, as demonstration is the middle for science and dialectical syllogism for opinion.
claims: The formal ratio of the incomplex object is that under which all credibles are attributed to God
The middle of assent to credibles is divine authority ruling the Church and revealing Scripture

jsnvu6-e182018-d1e609.summary: Reply to the first argument: though faith concerns God principally, it also concerns other things as attributed to God, so unbelief can concern either.
claims: Faith concerns created things insofar as they are related to God

jsnvu6-e182018-d1e620.summary: Reply to the second: God is charity's principal object, and neighbor is loved by charity only for God's sake, though another kind of friendship toward neighbor in himself is possible; likewise faith regards other things only as related to God.
claims: Neighbor is loved by charity only for God's sake
Faith regards creatures only in their relation to God

jsnvu6-e182018.summary: Question 1 of d.24 asks whether God is the object of faith. Durandus distinguishes faith in general (assent on a speaker's authority) from theological faith (assent to Scripture on God's authority), and the object as that about which something is believed (incomplex) or what is believed (complex). In the first sense God is the principal object, since everything believed is attributed to him. In the second sense the object is a proposition, since assent bears on complexes, and believers and unbelievers differ only in assent, not in grasping terms. All credibles resolve to one first credible: that the Church, and specifically the apostolic Church of eyewitnesses, is ruled by the Holy Spirit. Its approval grounds belief in Scripture's inspiration, and through Scripture the articles. Against those who make 'being unseen' faith's formal aspect, Durandus argues that a formal aspect cannot be negative, cannot lie on the knower's side, and cannot follow the act. Non-visibility is only a concomitant condition of faith in this life. The formal aspect is that under which credibles are attributed to God, and the middle of assent is divine authority ruling the Church and revealing Scripture.
claims: God is the principal, incomplex object of faith as that to which all credibles are attributed
What is believed is a complex proposition
All credibles resolve to belief that the Church is ruled by the Holy Spirit
Scripture is believed inspired because the apostolic Church approved it
Being unseen is a concomitant condition, not the formal ratio, of faith's object
The middle of assent in faith is divine authority ruling the Church and revealing Scripture
